Configuration & Secrets: ConfigMaps & Secrets; injecting configuration into pods

slides.title: ConfigMaps And Secrets
slides.lead:
Container images stay fixed, but applications often need different settings per environment, like a database address
Kubernetes stores such values outside the image in two objects: ConfigMap for plain settings, Secret for sensitive data

points.text: ConfigMap holds key-value pairs: log level, API URL
Secret holds sensitive data: passwords, tokens, certificates

slides.notes: "Compare the image to the exam paper and the ConfigMap or Secret to the centre's slip. Secrets specifically protect credentials, unlike plain ConfigMaps. Ask why hardcoding a password in the image is risky."

slides.title: ConfigMaps And Secrets

points.text: Both created from literals, files or YAML manifests
Pods reference them by name, not hardcoded values

slides.notes: "Compare the image to the exam paper and the ConfigMap or Secret to the centre's slip. Secrets specifically protect credentials, unlike plain ConfigMaps. Ask why hardcoding a password in the image is risky."

slides.label: Analogy: one question paper, a slip per centre
slides.title: ConfigMaps And Secrets
slides.notes: TR analogy: A college prints one common question paper for every centre, but each centre pastes a slip with its room number: just as a ConfigMap attaches environment settings without changing the image. "Compare the image to the exam paper and the ConfigMap or Secret to the centre's slip. Secrets specifically protect credentials, unlike plain ConfigMaps. Ask why hardcoding a password in the image is risky."

slides.title: Storage And Encoding
slides.lead: Both share a key-value structure, but Kubernetes stores and protects their contents differently once saved to the cluster
slides.notes: "Point to the encoding row: base64 is encoding, not encryption, a common interview trap. Mention enabling etcd encryption at rest for genuine protection. Ask why base64 alone does not secure a Secret."

slides.title: Storage And Encoding

points.text: Secrets are encrypted at rest only if etcd encryption is enabled
Secrets stay hidden from plain kubectl describe output
ConfigMaps stay unencrypted by design since data is non-sensitive

slides.notes: "Point to the encoding row: base64 is encoding, not encryption, a common interview trap. Mention enabling etcd encryption at rest for genuine protection. Ask why base64 alone does not secure a Secret."

slides.title: Env Vars Vs Volumes
slides.lead: Pods consume ConfigMap and Secret data in two ways, chosen by how the application reads its settings and whether updates must apply without a restart

points.text: envFrom or valueFrom injects keys as environment variables
Volume mount exposes each key as a file in a directory

slides.notes: "Point out that environment variables need a pod restart to pick up a change, but mounted files update live through kubelet sync. Ask how a hot-reloading application should consume a ConfigMap."

slides.title: Env Vars Vs Volumes

points.text: Env vars are fixed at container start, frozen until restart
Volume-mounted files sync automatically when the source object changes

slides.notes: "Point out that environment variables need a pod restart to pick up a change, but mounted files update live through kubelet sync. Ask how a hot-reloading application should consume a ConfigMap."

slides.title: Secrets Manager Bridge
slides.lead: On Amazon EKS, the AWS Secrets Store CSI Driver can mount secrets held directly in AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store as pod volumes, avoiding a second copy in the cluster

points.text: Centralizes rotation and audit logging outside the Kubernetes cluster
The SecretProviderClass is namespace-scoped, usable only by pods in that namespace

slides.notes: "Point to the AWS Secrets Manager console as the real source of truth the CSI driver pulls from. Mention this avoids storing sensitive data twice. Ask how this driver differs from a plain Kubernetes Secret."

slides.title: Secrets Manager Bridge

points.text: Mounted secrets refresh on a poll interval when rotation is enabled, so no pod restart is needed

note.text: With configuration externalized safely, the next concern is routing outside traffic into the cluster and organising workloads into namespaces

slides.notes: "Point to the AWS Secrets Manager console as the real source of truth the CSI driver pulls from. Mention this avoids storing sensitive data twice. Ask how this driver differs from a plain Kubernetes Secret."
Ingress & Namespaces: Ingress controllers & routing rules; namespaces; resource requests, limits & quotas

slides.title: Routing And Isolation
slides.lead: Running many services in one cluster raises three questions: how traffic reaches the right service, how teams share the cluster safely, and how much compute each pod may use

points.text: Ingress: single entry point routing external traffic by host or path
Namespaces: virtual partitions separating teams, environments or projects
Resource requests, limits & quotas: governing how much compute each pod and namespace consumes

slides.notes: "Frame the section as three practical controls needed once a cluster runs many services. Mention that the AWS Load Balancer Controller handles Ingress on EKS, and the EKS console's Resources tab lists Namespaces. Interview angle: distinguish routing from resource governance."

slides.title: Single Traffic Entry
slides.lead:
Each LoadBalancer-type Service needs its own external balancer, costly once a cluster hosts many services
Ingress is an API object defining HTTP(S) routing rules so one entry point reaches many services

points.text: Rules match requests by hostname, path, or both
Reduces per-service cloud balancer cost at scale
Needs a controller running to take effect

slides.notes: "AWS EKS uses the AWS Load Balancer Controller to turn an Ingress object into an Application Load Balancer. LoadBalancer services create one balancer each; Ingress consolidates routing into one. Exam hook: Ingress alone does nothing without a controller."

slides.label: Analogy: office receptionist
slides.title: Single Traffic Entry
slides.notes: TR analogy: An office receptionist directs each visitor to the right floor by name: just as Ingress routes each request to the right service by hostname or path. "AWS EKS uses the AWS Load Balancer Controller to turn an Ingress object into an Application Load Balancer. LoadBalancer services create one balancer each; Ingress consolidates routing into one. Exam hook: Ingress alone does nothing without a controller."

slides.title: Host And Path Rules
slides.lead: An Ingress object alone defines no behaviour; an Ingress controller, which runs inside the cluster, reads these objects and configures real routing

points.text: Ingress controller: AWS Load Balancer Controller, HAProxy, Traefik or another implementation of the rules
Host-based routing: separate domains, e.g. shop.example.com, api.example.com, to different services
Path-based routing: one domain, with /orders and /cart sent to different services

slides.notes: "Explain the controller watches the API server for Ingress objects and updates its proxy configuration live. Point to the EKS console's Load Balancers page showing the ALB created from an Ingress. Mention Gateway API as the newer successor, and that the community Ingress NGINX project was retired in March 2026. Interview hook: Ingress needs a controller installed, the object alone does nothing."

slides.title: Host And Path Rules

points.text: TLS termination: controller can decrypt HTTPS before forwarding to pods
On EKS, AWS Load Balancer Controller provisions an Application Load Balancer per Ingress

slides.notes: "Explain the controller watches the API server for Ingress objects and updates its proxy configuration live. Point to the EKS console's Load Balancers page showing the ALB created from an Ingress. Mention Gateway API as the newer successor, and that the community Ingress NGINX project was retired in March 2026. Interview hook: Ingress needs a controller installed, the object alone does nothing."

slides.title: Cluster Virtual Partitions
slides.lead:
A cluster shared by many teams risks name clashes
A namespace is a virtual partition inside one cluster, scoping object names so same-named resources coexist safely

points.text: Distinct from Linux kernel namespaces: groups objects, not processes
Default namespaces include default, kube-system and kube-public

slides.notes: "This differs from Linux process namespaces, a cluster-level grouping, not process isolation. Point to the EKS console's Namespaces list. Exam hook: a Pod name must be unique only within its namespace."

slides.title: Cluster Virtual Partitions

points.text: Most API objects, like Pods and Services, live inside a namespace
Nodes and persistent volumes stay cluster-scoped, outside any namespace

slides.notes: "This differs from Linux process namespaces, a cluster-level grouping, not process isolation. Point to the EKS console's Namespaces list. Exam hook: a Pod name must be unique only within its namespace."

slides.label: Analogy: classrooms with their own registers
slides.title: Cluster Virtual Partitions
slides.notes: TR analogy: A school campus splits students into separate classrooms in one building, each keeping its own attendance register: just as a namespace keeps names private within its own slice of one cluster. "This differs from Linux process namespaces, a cluster-level grouping, not process isolation. Point to the EKS console's Namespaces list. Exam hook: a Pod name must be unique only within its namespace."

slides.title: Isolation In Practice
slides.lead: Namespaces let one cluster serve several environments or teams without separate clusters, because access and quotas can be scoped per namespace rather than per cluster

points.text: Team separation: each team manages its own namespace, avoiding name conflicts
DNS-based discovery: name.namespace.svc.cluster.local reaches a service in another namespace
Resource quotas apply per namespace, capping total compute for that group

slides.notes: "Namespaces are a logical boundary for names and quotas, not automatically a security wall. Point to the EKS console dropdown that filters resources by namespace. Interview hook: cross-namespace calls need the namespace in the name (name.namespace); same-namespace calls do not."

slides.title: Per-Pod Compute Bounds
slides.lead:
Without a bound, one pod can starve others on shared CPU and memory
A request guarantees compute at scheduling; a limit sets the ceiling it may never exceed

points.text: Scheduler places a pod only where requested capacity is free
CPU limit exceeded: pod is throttled, not killed

slides.notes: "This builds on cgroups from container fundamentals, enforcing requests and limits at the node. The EKS console shows usage against these values under Pod details. Exam hook: CPU throttles under a limit; memory is killed."

slides.title: Per-Pod Compute Bounds

points.text: Memory limit exceeded: container is OOMKilled, then restarted per its restart policy
Units: CPU in millicores (500m), memory in mebibytes (256Mi)

slides.notes: "This builds on cgroups from container fundamentals, enforcing requests and limits at the node. The EKS console shows usage against these values under Pod details. Exam hook: CPU throttles under a limit; memory is killed."

slides.label: Analogy: hostel mess plates
slides.title: Per-Pod Compute Bounds
slides.notes: TR analogy: A hostel mess guarantees every student one full plate, but no one can take more than two plates. In the same way, a request guarantees a pod its minimum compute, and a limit caps the maximum it can use. "This builds on cgroups from container fundamentals, enforcing requests and limits at the node. The EKS console shows usage against these values under Pod details. Exam hook: CPU throttles under a limit; memory is killed."

slides.title: Capping Namespace Totals
slides.lead:
Individual pod limits do not stop a namespace from launching unlimited pods
A ResourceQuota object caps the total CPU, memory, and object count a namespace may consume across all its pods

cells: Caps total CPU, memory, object count

slides.notes: "Point to the EKS console's ResourceQuotas view under a selected namespace, showing used versus hard caps. Interview hook: a ResourceQuota can require every pod to declare requests and limits, rejecting ones that do not."

slides.title: Capping Namespace Totals
slides.lead: Ingress decides who can reach the cluster, namespaces decide who shares it, and quotas decide how much each group may use: together they keep a multi-service cluster reachable and fair
slides.notes: "Point to the EKS console's ResourceQuotas view under a selected namespace, showing used versus hard caps. Interview hook: a ResourceQuota can require every pod to declare requests and limits, rejecting ones that do not."

Mid-session quiz (sections 1-2). Q1. Which object holds plain settings and which holds sensitive data? Answer: ConfigMap for plain settings, Secret for sensitive data. Q2. Is a Secret encrypted in etcd by default? Answer: No, it is base64-encoded, not encrypted, unless etcd encryption is enabled. Q3. Which way of injecting a ConfigMap picks up a change without a restart? Answer: The volume mount, whose files sync automatically. Q4. What does an Ingress object need running before it takes effect? Answer: An Ingress controller. Q5. Must a Pod name be unique across the whole cluster? Answer: No, only within its namespace. Q6. What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit? Answer: It is OOMKilled, then restarted per its restart policy.
Health & Self-Healing: Liveness, readiness & startup probes

slides.title: Self-Healing Blind Spot
slides.lead:
Self-healing restarts a container only when its process actually exits; a container that hangs but keeps running looks healthy to that check
Probes let the kubelet test real application health instead

points.text: Liveness probe: detects a hung container, triggers a restart
Readiness probe: detects a not-yet-ready pod, holds traffic back
Startup probe: delays the other two for slow-starting applications

slides.notes: "Point out that the crash-only restart from the earlier restart-policy slide cannot see a hung application. Explain each probe answers a different health question. Interview hook: ask why a hung process escapes a crash-only restart."

slides.label: Analogy: a frozen phone screen
slides.title: Self-Healing Blind Spot
slides.notes: TR analogy: A frozen phone screen still looks switched on until you tap it, just as a hung container still looks running until a probe checks if it actually responds. "Point out that the crash-only restart from the earlier restart-policy slide cannot see a hung application. Explain each probe answers a different health question. Interview hook: ask why a hung process escapes a crash-only restart."

slides.title: How Checks Run
slides.lead: Each probe runs on a schedule set in the pod manifest and takes one of several forms, the three most common shown here, with shared threshold fields deciding when a result counts as failure

cells: kubelet calls a URL path, 200-399 is healthy
kubelet runs a command inside the container

slides.notes: "Point to a kubectl get pod -o yaml output, naming these same fields. Mention that the workload view in EKS, AKS or GKE surfaces probe failures as pod events. Exam hook: name a probe mechanism and its matching manifest field."

slides.title: How Checks Run

points.text: periodSeconds: how often the kubelet repeats the check
failureThreshold: consecutive failures before an action triggers
initialDelaySeconds: wait before the very first check runs

slides.notes: "Point to a kubectl get pod -o yaml output, naming these same fields. Mention that the workload view in EKS, AKS or GKE surfaces probe failures as pod events. Exam hook: name a probe mechanism and its matching manifest field."

slides.title: Restart Trace
slides.lead: A worked timeline on one pod shows the threshold being crossed and the consequence it triggers, while a separate readiness check runs on the same pod independently

points.text: t=0s: container starts on port 8080, startup probe gates the other two
t=10s, 20s, 30s: liveness probe at http://pod-ip:8080/healthz times out thrice, periodSeconds=10
failureThreshold=3 reached: kubelet kills and restarts only this container

slides.notes: "Walk the timeline, stressing liveness restarts only the container while readiness only pulls the pod from traffic. Point to kubectl describe pod events showing Unhealthy and Killing entries. Interview hook: ask why a failing readiness probe never causes a restart."

slides.title: Restart Trace

points.text: Readiness probe fails separately: pod removed from Service endpoints, no restart
Container restarts, passes checks, pod rejoins Service endpoints

note.text: The readiness gate seen here is what a rolling update relies on to avoid downtime: a new pod receives traffic only once it is ready

slides.notes: "Walk the timeline, stressing liveness restarts only the container while readiness only pulls the pod from traffic. Point to kubectl describe pod events showing Unhealthy and Killing entries. Interview hook: ask why a failing readiness probe never causes a restart."
Rolling Updates & Rollback: Update strategy; surge & unavailability settings; rollback of a bad release

slides.title: Recreate Vs RollingUpdate
slides.lead:
Deploying a new image to every pod at once takes the application offline until new pods start
A Deployment's spec chooses between two strategies, RollingUpdate (default) and Recreate, to control that switch

points.text: Recreate: terminates all old pods before starting new ones
RollingUpdate: new pods added while old pods removed gradually

slides.notes: "Explain that Recreate causes a visible outage while RollingUpdate does not, and point to the strategy type field in a Deployment manifest. Exam angle: why RollingUpdate is the default for stateless web services."

slides.title: Recreate Vs RollingUpdate

points.text: Rollout progress visible on the Deployment's EKS console page
RollingUpdate keeps the service reachable throughout the rollout

slides.notes: "Explain that Recreate causes a visible outage while RollingUpdate does not, and point to the strategy type field in a Deployment manifest. Exam angle: why RollingUpdate is the default for stateless web services."

slides.label: Analogy: repaving one lane at a time
slides.title: Recreate Vs RollingUpdate
slides.notes: TR analogy: A highway repaving crew closes one lane at a time and reroutes traffic rather than shutting the whole road: just as a rolling update replaces pods lane by lane while the service stays reachable. "Explain that Recreate causes a visible outage while RollingUpdate does not, and point to the strategy type field in a Deployment manifest. Exam angle: why RollingUpdate is the default for stateless web services."

slides.title: Controlling Rollout Pace
slides.lead: With 6 replicas and both fields at 25%, Kubernetes adds 2 extra pods first, then takes old pods down one at a time
slides.notes: "Walk through the table: with 6 replicas and 25 percent, surge rounds up to 2 extra pods and unavailable rounds down to 1. Ask why Kubernetes biases rounding toward availability over strict pod count, a common interview probe."

slides.title: Controlling Rollout Pace

cells: Extra pods allowed above desired count

slides.notes: "Walk through the table: with 6 replicas and 25 percent, surge rounds up to 2 extra pods and unavailable rounds down to 1. Ask why Kubernetes biases rounding toward availability over strict pod count, a common interview probe."

slides.title: Reverting Prior Revision
slides.lead: Deployments keep a revision history of past ReplicaSets, so a release that fails its probes or breaks in production can be reverted to the last known-good version

points.text: kubectl rollout history shows past revision numbers
kubectl rollout undo reverts to the previous ReplicaSet

slides.notes: "Point to the Deployments tab on an EKS console after a bad image tag fails readiness checks, then run rollout undo live. Exam hook: rollback reuses the same rolling mechanism, just in the reverse direction."

slides.title: Reverting Prior Revision

points.text: rollout undo --to-revision=N targets a specific older version
Old ReplicaSet scales up, bad one scales down automatically

slides.notes: "Point to the Deployments tab on an EKS console after a bad image tag fails readiness checks, then run rollout undo live. Exam hook: rollback reuses the same rolling mechanism, just in the reverse direction."
Managed Kubernetes: EKS, AKS & GKE; provider-managed components; self-managed vs managed trade-offs

slides.title: Who Runs Control Plane
slides.lead: Running a Kubernetes cluster independently means installing and operating every control-plane component directly; a managed service removes that operational burden

points.text: Self-managed: team installs, patches and scales the control plane
Managed: cloud provider operates the control plane components
Three major managed services: EKS, AKS, GKE
Cluster nodes still run customer workloads either way

slides.notes: "Contrast running Kubernetes on self-managed virtual machines against paying AWS, Azure or Google to run it. Mention that most production teams take the managed path since it is the focus here. An interviewer may ask who patches etcd in a managed cluster: the provider does."

slides.title: What Provider Operates
slides.lead: A managed Kubernetes service operates the API server, scheduler, controller manager and etcd on infrastructure it owns, patches and keeps highly available

points.text: Provider handles patching, upgrades and control-plane high availability
Customer still manages workload manifests and add-ons
Plus worker nodes unless a serverless option such as Fargate is chosen

slides.notes: "Point out that only the control-plane pieces move to the provider; the worker nodes stay visible in the EKS or GKE console. Say that kubectl still talks to the same API server endpoint, just one the team never patches. Expect an interview question on exactly which components a managed service covers."

slides.title: What Provider Operates

points.text: Provider exposes only the API server endpoint to connect kubectl
AWS console shows this as the EKS cluster endpoint field

slides.notes: "Point out that only the control-plane pieces move to the provider; the worker nodes stay visible in the EKS or GKE console. Say that kubectl still talks to the same API server endpoint, just one the team never patches. Expect an interview question on exactly which components a managed service covers."

slides.label: Analogy: a rented flat
slides.title: What Provider Operates
slides.notes: TR analogy: A rented flat's owner takes care of the building, lift and water supply, while you only manage your own furniture and belongings, just as a managed Kubernetes service runs the control plane while your team manages only its apps. "Point out that only the control-plane pieces move to the provider; the worker nodes stay visible in the EKS or GKE console. Say that kubectl still talks to the same API server endpoint, just one the team never patches. Expect an interview question on exactly which components a managed service covers."

slides.title: Provider Offerings Compared
slides.lead: Each hyperscaler sells the same managed-control-plane idea under its own name, differing mainly in how worker nodes are provisioned

cells: Managed node groups, Fargate serverless pods or EKS Auto Mode
Virtual machine scale sets as node pools
Autopilot fully managed nodes or Standard mode

slides.notes: "Walk through the table left to right: AWS, Azure and Google each offer the same idea under a different name. Mention the EKS console's node-group screen and GKE's Autopilot toggle as where this choice is actually made. An interviewer may ask to name the three services and their parent clouds."

slides.title: Trade-Offs To Weigh
slides.lead: Choosing between running an own control plane and paying a provider to run it trades operational effort against cost and control

cells: Team patches etcd, API server, upgrades
No control-plane fee, higher staff time
Often a per-cluster control-plane fee (varies by provider and tier), plus node cost
Team builds HA etcd and API server
Provider offers a control-plane uptime SLA

slides.notes: "Frame this as a cost-versus-control decision rather than a right-or-wrong choice. Mention that a regulated on-premises workload often forces self-managed, while most teams pick managed to save operational effort. Expect a question asking to justify one choice over the other for a given scenario."

Quiz on Kubernetes in Practice. Q1. Why is base64 alone not enough to secure a Secret? Answer: Base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone who reads it can decode it. Q2. Which two fields route a request in an Ingress rule? Answer: The hostname and the path. Q3. Which probe pulls a pod from Service endpoints without restarting it? Answer: The readiness probe. Q4. With failureThreshold=3 and periodSeconds=10, how long until a hung container is restarted? Answer: About 30 seconds, after three failed checks. Q5. With 6 replicas and 25%, how many extra pods may maxSurge add? Answer: 2, because surge rounds up. Q6. Which command reverts a Deployment to its previous ReplicaSet? Answer: kubectl rollout undo. Q7. In a managed cluster, who patches etcd? Answer: The provider.
